title: Comodor application protocol
description: The one definition of what Comodor Core and a Comodor client say to each other. Python types and TypeScript types are both generated from this file by tools/protocol-codegen.py; neither is edited by hand, and a test regenerates both and fails on any difference. That is the whole mechanism by which the two sides cannot silently disagree.

x-envelope.description: One JSON object per line, UTF-8, no embedded newlines. Four shapes, distinguished by `type`. An event also carries `seq`: the session's own monotonic counter, starting at 1, which is what makes a snapshot and a live stream reconcilable rather than merely usually consistent.

x-errors.parse_error: The line was not JSON, or not an object.
x-errors.invalid_envelope: JSON, but not one of the four shapes.
x-errors.unsupported_version: The client asked for a protocol version this core does not speak.
x-errors.not_initialized: A method other than client.hello arrived before the handshake.
x-errors.invalid_params: The method exists; the parameters do not fit it.
x-errors.unknown_request: No pending question or permission with that id.
x-errors.not_allowed: The mode or permission policy refused it.
x-errors.internal_error: A fault in the core. The message is safe to show; details go to stderr.

x-capabilities.description: What each side can do, exchanged at the handshake. A name absent from the list means not supported; a name present that the other side does not know is ignored. Neither side may assume a capability it did not see.

client.hello.summary: The handshake. Must be first; every other method is refused until it succeeds.

session.create.summary: Open a session. The workspace defaults to the core's working directory.

session.get.summary: The authoritative state of one session, for a client that has just connected or reconnected.

session.snapshot.summary: The whole visible session, including its conversation, tools and any pending question — for a client rebuilding its own state while the core keeps the session.

session.history.summary: Earlier conversations from the shared store, newest first. Lives on disk, unlike `session.list`, which serves the process's live sessions.

session.open.summary: Reopen a stored conversation as a live session: transcript, plan and title restored; running delegates stay lost on their own record. Opening one already open hands back the live session.

session.send.summary: Send a message. Returns as soon as the turn is accepted; the answer arrives as events.

session.cancel.summary: Stop whatever the session is doing. Answers whether there was anything to stop.

session.set_mode.summary: Change what the agent is allowed to do. The core is the authority; the client renders what comes back.

model.get.summary: Which provider and model this session answers with. Never includes a credential.

model.list.summary: The models the active provider can name, for a chooser. Always includes the configured model; a provider that cannot enumerate yields just that one. Never includes a credential.

workspace.get.summary: The directory the agent is pointed at.

question.answer.summary: Answer a structured question the agent asked.

permission.reply.summary: Allow or refuse a tool call the agent is waiting on.

delegate.stop.summary: Ask the core to stop one running background delegate. The core is the authority: it answers whether there was anything to stop, and the delegate's actual state arrives as `delegate.updated` events — `stopping` first, then the terminal state the worker settles on. A client must not paint a final state this method returned.

shutdown.summary: Close every session and stop. The core answers, then exits.

Mode.description: What the agent is allowed to do. Enforced by the core, not by the client.

MessageStatus.description: How a message stands. `streaming` means it is still open and more deltas can arrive: a snapshot taken mid-answer must say so, because a client that read an unfinished message as `completed` would stop listening to it. `cancelled` and `failed` are not decoration: a client that cannot tell them from `completed` has to leave a stopped answer looking like one still arriving.

ToolState.description: Where one tool invocation has got to.

RiskLevel.description: The tier a tool declares, and the reason it is asking. `safe` reads, `write` changes files, `dangerous` runs commands or reaches the network. A client shows it so the person can see what kind of thing they are approving; it is the core's own classification, not a guess the client makes from the tool's name.

InteractionKind.description: Which sort of blocking interaction is waiting on a person. A question wants information; a permission wants authorization.

Empty.description: A method that takes nothing. Still an object, so a parameter can be added later without a new shape.

PeerInfo.description: Who is on the other end. Reported, never trusted for authorisation.

Session.description: A session as the core knows it. This is the authoritative shape a client resynchronises against.

SnapshotMessage.description: One message as the core has it. `text` is the whole message, not a delta: a snapshot replaces a projection rather than adding to one.

started_seq.description: The session sequence number of the event that put this message into the timeline. Messages and tools are ordered by this one shared domain rather than by their position in two separate arrays, which is what makes a rebuilt session interleave them the way the live stream did.

SnapshotTool.description: One tool invocation as the core has it. `output` is what the core still holds, which is capped; `output_truncated` says so rather than letting a client present a shortened transcript as the whole one.

started_seq.description: The session sequence number of the `tool.started` event. Ordered against messages in the same domain, so a rebuilt turn reads message, tool, message rather than every message followed by every tool.

TaskState.description: Where one item of the agent's own plan stands. The vocabulary is the `todo_write` tool's, not the interface's: a client renders these four and invents no others — a frontend-only state such as `queued` would be a claim the core never made.

TaskItem.description: One item of the agent's task list. Tasks carry no id: the list is small, the tool replaces it whole on every update, and an index is not an identity across a replacement. A client that renders the list in order needs nothing more; a future operation on one task would need a real core-owned id, which this deliberately does not fake.

TasksUpdated.description: The agent's whole task list, as `todo_write` recorded it. Replacement, never addition: a task the new list does not carry is gone, and the order is the order the model wrote. Arrives on the session's sequence like every other event, so a snapshot and a live stream converge on the same list.

DelegateState.description: Where one background delegate has got to. `running` and `stopping` are the live states; the other four are terminal and a delegate never comes back from one. `lost` is the honest state of a delegate that was running when the process died: it is reported after a reload rather than pretended to be alive. A state only ever moves forward through this vocabulary — a late announcement cannot walk one backwards.

Delegate.description: One background delegate, as the core's manager knows it. Every field is a fact the core already keeps: no progress percentage is invented, and `steps`, `tool_calls` and `tokens` are what the worker recorded — zero until it settles, because a running delegate has not reported anything yet. `elapsed` is seconds as of this record; `started_at` is the core's epoch seconds, which lets a client tick a running delegate's clock without asking. `label` is the model's own short name for the work (or the head of its brief) — display text, not a promise.

DelegateUpdated.description: One background delegate moved. The whole record rides along, so a client replaces what it holds for that id rather than merging fields — and applies the state vocabulary's forward-only rule: an event cannot move a delegate back from `stopping` to `running` or out of a terminal state.

DelegateStopResult.description: Whether there was a running delegate to stop. `false` is an honest answer, not an error: the delegate may have finished in the instant the request arrived, or never existed. What it actually became arrives as `delegate.updated` — `stopping` when the stop took, then the terminal state the worker settles on. Stopping every delegate at once is deliberately not a protocol operation: one deliberate stop is the surface F5 promises.

SessionSnapshot.description: Everything a client needs to draw a session it did not watch happen. `revision` is the sequence number this state includes up to: the client drops any event at or below it and applies the rest, which is what makes rebuilding safe while the session is still streaming. Every message and tool carries `started_seq`, the sequence at which it entered the timeline, so the two lists merge into the one order the live stream had rather than being drawn messages-then-tools. `tasks` and `delegates` carry the workbench state the same way: a client that mounts mid-job sees the plan and the delegated work without replaying history, and a client too old to know them ignores them.

tasks.description: The agent's current task list, whole. The `todo_write` tool replaces the entire list on every update, and so does this: a snapshot's tasks are the list, not an addition to whatever a client already held.

delegates.description: Every background delegate this session knows, terminal ones included, so a client rebuilding after a crash sees the honest `lost` rather than an empty panel. A delegate that was running when the process died is here as `lost`.

question.description: The first question waiting, for a client that presents one interaction at a time. `interactions` is the complete list and is what a client should prefer.

permission.description: The first permission waiting, for a client that presents one interaction at a time. `interactions` is the complete list and is what a client should prefer.

interactions.description: Everything waiting on a person, oldest first. Two can be live at once: a batch of read-only tools may run in parallel and each ask a question, and a delegate shares its parent's event bus. Carrying only one would silently strand the other, which is why this list exists alongside the singular fields.

PendingInteraction.description: One blocking interaction a snapshot is carrying. Exactly one of `question` or `permission` is present, and `kind` says which, so a client can narrow without inspecting both.

AcceptedResult.description: The turn was accepted. `turn_id` correlates every message.* and tool.* event it produces. It is a turn and not a message because one turn interleaves several assistant messages with the tools between them, and naming it after the first would make the rest look like repeats of it.

ModelResult.description: Never carries a key. `configured` is how a client shows that a provider needs setting up without being told the secret.

QuestionOption.description: One row a person can pick. `id` is what travels back in `chosen`. `free` marks the write-your-own row, which carries typed text instead of a fixed label and is rendered differently.

QuestionRequest.description: A form the agent is waiting on, as a protocol primitive rather than a numbered list in prose. It carries *several* questions because the agent asks several at once — one round trip rather than four — so a client renders a form, not a prompt.

PermissionRequest.description: A tool call waiting on a person. `detail` is what the core already renders for a human; it is not a command to run. `tool` and `risk` are the context an informed decision needs — which capability is asking, and which tier it belongs to — and are optional so a core that has nothing truthful to say omits them rather than inventing a value.

tool.description: The tool that asked, by the name the core knows it as.

MessageStarted.description: A new assistant message within a turn. Each one has its own `message_id`; `turn_id` is shared by every event the same `session.send` caused.

MessageDelta.description: One piece of a streamed answer, routed by `message_id` alone. `channel` separates the answer from extended thinking, so a client can show or hide reasoning without guessing from the text.

MessageCompleted.description: The message is finished, one way or another. `text` is the whole answer where there is one, so a client that lost a delta is corrected rather than left with a gap. `error` accompanies `status: failed` and is written to be shown.

ToolOutput.description: Incremental output from a running tool, such as a shell command's lines as they arrive. `call_id` is required: the core binds the running call to the thread producing the output, so output from tools running in parallel cannot be attributed to whichever started last.

Notification.description: Something worth saying that is not part of an answer. `level` is advisory; a client may style it.

QuestionField.description: One question within a form. `header` is its stable name and is what an answer is matched on — not the position, which would silently reattach every answer if a question were reordered.

QuestionAnswer.description: What came back for one question. `chosen` holds option ids; `written` holds what was typed into the free row.

ModelListResult.description: A model chooser's source of truth. `models` is the provider's own list with the configured model guaranteed present; it is never empty when a model is configured.

Usage.description: How full the context is, and what the conversation has cost so far. Every field is optional because a provider that cannot measure one still reports the rest — a local model has no honest cost, and a client must show nothing rather than invent one.

SessionHistoryEntry.description: One stored conversation as a picker lists it. No transcript in the list — that is what `session.open` restores.
